title: Saxophone Giant Sonny Rollins Has Died at 95 — But His Music Will Roar Forever
summary: Have you ever heard a saxophone sound so big and bold it felt like a whole parade? That was Sonny Rollins. He died on Monday at age 95, but his music will keep roaring for generations. Rollins was a jazz legend who played the tenor saxophone with a tone so powerful you could recognize it in just a couple of seconds. He grew up in Harlem, New York, surrounded by other future jazz stars. But even when he became famous, he never stopped searching for new sounds. In the late 1950s, he took a break from performing and practiced alone on the Williamsburg Bridge at night — just him and his horn, with the city lights below. When he returned, his album The Bridge became a huge event. Rollins didn't just play fast, tricky jazz. He loved catchy tunes, too, like calypso songs and even a Stevie Wonder hit. He said the best music came when he forgot everything he practiced and just let the music play him. That's like a basketball player who stops thinking and just sinks the shot. Rollins won big awards, but he said the real reward was doing the work. So next time you hear a saxophone wailing, think of Sonny Rollins — the man who made his horn sing with his whole heart.
why_it_matters: Sonny Rollins' story shows that deep dedication and a love for practice can turn you into a legend — your own 'bridge' might be whatever quiet place helps you get better at what you love.

keywords.explanation: A tenor saxophone is a large curved saxophone that produces a warm, powerful sound, often used in jazz.
Calypso is a joyful, bouncy music style from the Caribbean islands that makes you think of sunshine and dancing.
The Bridge is a famous jazz album by Sonny Rollins that he made after secretly practicing on a bridge for many nights.
The Williamsburg Bridge is a big bridge in New York City connecting Brooklyn and Manhattan, and Sonny Rollins used it as his private practice room.
Harlem is a neighborhood in New York City known for its rich African American culture and many great musicians.
In jazz, musicians often call their saxophone or trumpet a 'horn' as a nickname for their instrument.

background_read: Sonny Rollins (1930–2025) was one of the most powerful tenor saxophonists in jazz history, known for his huge, roaring sound.
The Williamsburg Bridge is a busy bridge in New York City, and Rollins chose to practice there late at night so he wouldn't bother his neighbors in Harlem.
Stevie Wonder (a famous singer and songwriter) wrote the hit 'Isn't She Lovely,' and Rollins liked to play his catchy tunes to connect with everyday listeners.
Article_Structure: WHO: Sonny Rollins, a saxophone giant who died at age 95.
WHAT: He had a powerful, instantly recognizable sound, practiced alone on a bridge at night, and made timeless albums like The Bridge, mixing jazz with calypso and pop.
WHERE: From his childhood in Harlem to the Williamsburg Bridge, New York shaped his music.
WHY: To celebrate a life devoted to searching for new sounds and to remind us that real rewards come from the work itself, not just awards.

perspectives.description: Many musicians see Rollins as a hero because he practiced alone for hours to find his voice, proving that hard work is more valuable than fame.
Some modern critics might say his long solos were too long and that his sound belongs to an older era that isn't as popular today.
His habit of playing calypso and Stevie Wonder songs shows how jazz has always absorbed other styles to survive and stay fresh.
